#### Description

query.intent:
tsdb: preserve exemplars across compaction and restart

#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:
Compaction can remove a series after its last sample is persisted, even when it still has a recent exemplar. Because exemplars are not stored in blocks, they depend on WAL replay for recovery. If WAL cleanup drops the series identity while retaining its exemplar record, the exemplar is lost on restart.

This change tracks each series’ latest accepted exemplar timestamp and preserves its identity until the exemplar falls below the replay cutoff. The protection applies to ordinary, selected, and stale compaction, and is restored when loading the WAL or a memory snapshot.

Selected and stale compaction still release persisted sample chunks and their appenders when safe, while retaining the identity needed for exemplar recovery. Existing protections for concurrent appends and out-of-order samples remain in place.

query.intent:
Optimize module reloading check

Check each module once when deciding whether to reload a cached module

## Description

When a module that has already been parsed is imported again, `parse_module_file` calls `module_needs_reloading` to check whether any file in the module's tree has changed on disk. That walk recurses through `submodules` and `imported_modules` without tracking which modules it has visited, so a module reachable through several paths is re-read once per *path*.

That's common in practice: a `mod.nu` that `export use`s its sibling files, where most siblings also `use` a few shared helpers. In the repro from the issue, every extra `use nested` of a 9-file module re-reads its files ~133 times; with a real 22-file library it's ~412 reads per import. Linux mostly hides this because file opens are cheap, but on Windows it dominates parse time, and the LSP pays it on every keystroke.

This PR adds a `seen` set for the duration of the walk, so each reachable module's file is read at most once per check. Skipping an already-seen module is safe: `any()` short-circuits on the first change, so a module seen again has already been found unchanged. I also extracted the read-and-compare into a separate `module_file_changed` function.

| 2 | 51.2 ms | 29.2 ms |

fix: reject out-of-range decimals in into string

## Description

`into string -d <precision>` panics when the precision is large enough that `10_f64.powi(precision as i32)` underflows to zero. The division then produces NaN, and `format!("{:.*}", precision, NaN)` panics with "Formatting argument out of range".

fix(v4): check array, set and map size bounds before parsing elements

Collapse toZod's enum leaf normalizer to a dummy union

Follow-up to #6528, from the request to find a smaller formulation than the mapped-key normalizer.

Fix long notebook magic assignments being wrapped in parentheses

### Description

When a notebook cell has a magic assignment that is longer than the line length, Black
wraps it in parentheses. For example this cell:

```python
installed_packages_in_this_environment = !pip list --format=freeze --disable-pip-version-check
```

becomes:

```python
installed_packages_in_this_environment = (
    !pip list --format=freeze --disable-pip-version-check
)
```

IPython does not accept a magic inside parentheses, so the cell now fails with
`SyntaxError: invalid syntax` when you run it. Black exits with 0, and later runs of
`black --check` also pass because Black skips the broken cell.

The reason is that Black formats the cell with each magic replaced by a placeholder
string. The placeholder can be wrapped like any other string, and the safety check only
sees the placeholder version, so it does not notice the problem.

The fix is in `unmask_cell`. After the magics are put back, it masks the cell again and
checks that IPython still finds the same magics. If it does not, the cell is left
unchanged, the same way Black already skips cells it cannot format safely.

I added tests for a long `!` assignment, a long `%timeit -o` assignment, an indented one,
and a direct test for `unmask_cell`. All of them fail without the fix.

Avoid quadratic runtime in right_hand_split_with_omits on long lines (#5270)

## Summary
Fixes #5270.
Closes #5275
Closes #5305

Formatting lines containing long chains of consecutive bracket trailers (such as subscript chains `a[0][1]...[160]`) suffered from quadratic runtime due to combinatorial omit trials in `right_hand_split_with_omits`.

### Root Cause
Unlike attribute chains which have dot delimiters and are split cleanly in a single pass by `delimiter_split`, consecutive
  subscript chains `][` have no intermediate delimiters and fall back to `right_hand_split_with_omits`.

`generate_trailers_to_omit` yields bracket pairs from the tail up to `line_length`. In long lines with many small trailers
  (like `[0]...`), Black was performing up to 20 full `right_hand_split` calls per recursion level, only for
  `is_line_short_enough(lines[0])` to fail on every single omit candidate because each candidate split point was still hundreds of
  characters from the start of the line.

### Fix
1. Precompute cumulative prefix lengths for all leaves in `line.leaves` once at the start of `right_hand_split_with_omits`.
2. For each candidate `omit`, inspect the target `opening_bracket` the split would break on. If its prefix length from the start of the line alone exceeds `mode.line_length`, any head line produced by that split is mathematically guaranteed to exceed `line_length`. We safely skip executing `right_hand_split` for that omit.
3. Candidate omits that break on an opening bracket within `mode.line_length` (e.g. `foo(long_args...)[key]`) are retained and evaluated normally.
4. In the final fallback, reuse `first_lines` instead of redundantly re-running `right_hand_split`.
5. Output formatting is 100% invariant across all cases (diff-shades shows 0 changes).

Track strikethrough (SGR 9) so it is not dropped across highlighted tokens

## Summary

`src/vscreen.rs` tracks the terminal's active ANSI style in an `Attributes` struct so bat can re-apply it before each syntax-highlighted token (nu_ansi_term appends a full `\x1B[0m` reset after every token). The struct already has a `strike` field, documented `ON: ^[9m / OFF: ^[29m`, that is initialized, cleared in `sgr_reset()`, and re-emitted in `Display` — but `update_with_sgr()` had **no match arm for SGR `9` or `29`**, so `strike` was only ever cleared, never set.

Consequence: with ANSI passthrough (the default — `--strip-ansi` and `--sanitize` both default to `never`), bold/dim/italic/underline survive across highlighted tokens because they are tracked and re-emitted, but strikethrough visibly disappears after the first token.

This adds the missing `9` (set) and `29` (clear) arms, mirroring the sibling underline (`4`/`24`) and italic (`3`/`23`) arms, so strikethrough persists like every other supported attribute. query.intent:
Perf/deserialize error path on failure

## Motivation

`Json`, `Form` and `Query` always deserialize through `serde_path_to_error`, which allocates for every field it visits so that it can report where an error happened. That's only useful when deserialization fails, but every successful request pays for it.

Measured in-process through `Router` on an M3 Pro, a POST with a three-field JSON body goes from 25 to 19 allocations and a two-field query from 22 to 18. In criterion that's 1.21x for receiving JSON, 1.24x for a form, 1.18x for a query and 1.12x for echoing JSON back, with an unrelated handler unchanged.

## Solution

Deserialize without path tracking first, and only if that fails do it again through `serde_path_to_error` to build the rejection. Error messages and rejection types stay the same, since the second pass sees the same input.

`Form` and `Query` share a small `deserialize_with_error_path` helper. `Json` does the same with `serde_json::from_slice` as the first attempt, since it also has to call `end()` on the deserializer to reject trailing input, which the helper can't do.

axum: only track the error path once deserialization has failed

bat prepends the arguments from its config file to the command line. So a user who keeps `--show-all` in `~/.config/bat/config` and then types `bat -A file` passes the flag twice, and clap rejects it:

```console

$ bat -A src/main.rs
error: the argument '--show-all' cannot be used multiple times

## Motivation

`PathRouter::merge` hands each of the other router's endpoints back to `route` or `route_service`. For `Endpoint::Route`, the endpoint is already a `Route`, but `route_service` wraps it in `Route::new` again. Each merge of a router that holds a service route (`route_service`, `nest_service` and so on) therefore adds another layer of boxing and a `RouteFuture`. Insert the existing `Route` with `route_endpoint` instead of calling `route_service`. Nothing else changes: the path is still validated and conflicts are still reported the same way.

The new test counts how many times a service is cloned while it handles a request, and checks that a merged service route is cloned as often as the same route used directly. Before this change it was cloned twice per request instead of once.

query.intent:
Use parsed CLI arguments to detect number flags

## Problem

Fix incorrect detection of `-n` / `-b` when these strings appear in positional arguments or option values.


`App::new()` currently scans `wild::args_os()` manually to determine whether `-n` or `-b` was supplied directly on the command line.

This scan does not implement clap's argument parsing rules. As a result, filenames after `--` and values belonging to short options can be interpreted as numbering flags.

For example:

```bash
printf 'hello\nworld\n' > ./-b
bat -- -b
```

The `-b` argument is a filename because it appears after the option terminator. However, the manual scanner treats it as `--number-nonblank`. This can change the output by forcing line numbers and disabling loop-through mode.

A similar problem occurs with short options that accept values:

```bash
bat -lbn input.txt
```

Here `bn` is the value of `-l`; it is not a combination of `-b` and `-n`.


The CLI-only flag detection was implemented separately from the clap command used to parse the final arguments. The manual scanner therefore does not handle:

- `--` option terminators;
- combined short options;
- short options with attached values;
- future changes to the argument definitions.

## Solution

Parse the original CLI arguments once with the existing clap command and use the resulting `ArgMatches` to determine whether `number` or `number-nonblank` was supplied directly by the user.

The existing config-file and environment-variable merging logic remains unchanged. The separately parsed matches are only used for CLI-only detection.

query.intent:
axum: Remove framing headers from successful CONNECT responses

## Motivation

For a 2xx response to `CONNECT`, `RouteFuture` quotes RFC 9110:

> A server MUST NOT send any Transfer-Encoding or Content-Length header fields in a 2xx (Successful) response to CONNECT.

It then replaces the body with `Body::empty()` but leaves the `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` headers in place. The response the router returns still carries the forbidden headers.

hyper's HTTP/1 encoder already drops these headers on the wire. Anything else that sees the response after the router still gets them: outer middleware, tests that call the router with `oneshot`, and servers that don't use hyper's HTTP/1 path.

## Solution

Remove `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` in the same branch that empties the body. I added a regression test, `successful_connect_drops_body_and_framing_headers`, which fails without the change.

Detect binary content beyond the first line

## Summary

- inspect up to the first 1024 already-buffered bytes before splitting out the first line
- preserve the reader's bytes, line boundaries, UTF-16 handling, and streaming behavior
- add regressions for cross-line binary detection, the 1024-byte boundary, single-read/EOF inputs, and the CLI binary header

Fixes #3554.

## Root cause

`content_inspector` checks up to 1024 bytes for a NUL byte, but bat passed only the first line. Random or encrypted data can contain a newline before its first NUL byte, so the shortened sample was classified as UTF-8 and binary bytes were sent to the terminal.

The fix snapshots the already-buffered prefix with `BufRead::fill_buf()` before `read_until` splits out the first line. The snapshot is non-consuming, so no bytes are lost or reordered, and it does not add a post-line blocking read. Empty input is handled without requesting a second EOF event.

## Compatibility

BOM detection still takes precedence, so UTF-16 input handling is unchanged. ZIP signature detection is also unchanged.

PR #3763 changes the same input initialization path for a distinct issue (#2262: bounding reads for newline-free binary files). If it merges first, this PR will need a small rebase, but the behaviors are complementary.

fix(axum-macros): use OptionalFromRequest for Option<T> fields

This supersedes #3665 and closes #3623 by implementing proper rejection mapping using OptionalFromRequest/OptionalFromRequestParts and adding regression tests for JSON parsing errors.



## Motivation

Currently, Option<T> fields in #[derive(FromRequest)] and #[derive(FromRequestParts)] use .ok() to handle the extracted result. This approach silently swallows all rejections (such as a JsonRejection when a payload is malformed or invalid) and converts them into None. The expected behavior is that an invalid payload should properly propagate its rejection to the client, and None should only be returned when the payload or part is genuinely missing (relying on the extractor's specific optional semantics).

## Solution

Replaced the .ok() chaining for Option<T> fields with the OptionalFromRequest and OptionalFromRequestParts traits. This delegates the decision of when to return None versus when to propagate a rejection directly to the specific extractor's implementation.

Additionally, added two regression tests (option_via_json.rs and option_via_parts.rs) to ensure that missing data gracefully resolves to None, while malformed data (like invalid JSON) properly surfaces the correct rejection/HTTP error.

body: Introduce Bodies of Unknown Size

As reported in <https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum/issues/3741>, in some responses to HEAD requests, the header `content-type: 0` would be included, even though the size of the body was not known and also not zero.

The reason for this was that `axum::body::Body::empty`, which represents a body that is *known to be empty* was used, even though *nothing was known about the body*.

To remedy, introduce a new utility type `axum::body::Unknown`, which represents an unknown body. This type could be considered for upstreaming to the `http-body-util` crate in the future.

## Motivation

The `FromRequest`, `FromRequestParts`, and `Handler` traits already use `#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]` to provide helpful compiler messages when users encounter trait bound errors. However, `IntoResponse` and `IntoResponseParts` — two of the most commonly encountered traits in error messages — lack this attribute.

When users forget to implement `IntoResponse` on their custom response types (or return types that don't implement it), the compiler shows a bare "trait bound not satisfied" error without guidance.

## Solution

Add `#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]` to both `IntoResponse` and `IntoResponseParts` traits in `axum-core`, with links to the relevant documentation pages. This matches the existing pattern used by the extractor and handler traits.

`bat --list-themes` unconditionally queried the terminal for its background

Follow-up to #3113. Three route-syntax bugs remained after it: a literal `\:` after a parameter was swallowed into the parameter name, `Remove` could not find escaped-colon routes, and reverse routing dropped the literal verb.

fix(router): share route syntax across routing operations

## Summary

Follow-up to #3113. Three route-syntax bugs remained after it: a literal `\:` after a parameter was swallowed into the parameter name, `Remove` could not find escaped-colon routes, and reverse routing dropped the literal verb.

query.intent:
fix(middleware): prevent BodyLimit bypass with contract-compliant readers

## Problem

With unknown `Content-Length`, `BodyLimit` forwarded an unbounded read to the underlying body. A caller that processes the returned `n > 0` bytes could receive more than the configured limit. The v4.15.2 JSON example in #3071 also accepted an oversized body. Current v5 uses `ReadFrom` followed by `json.Unmarshal` for default JSON binding, so that particular Bind bypass does not reproduce on v5; its read error was instead reported as HTTP 400.

- Reject negative `LimitBytes` in `ToMiddleware`.

This reader retains Echo's status-coded error contract. Unlike `http.MaxBytesReader`, it does not signal `net/http` to close the connection after overflow; that is existing BodyLimit behavior and can be evaluated separately.

query.intent:
fix: prevent completions from mutating os.Args via append side effect

## Summary

- Fixes a bug where `getCompletions()` accidentally mutates `os.Args` by writing `"--"` into the shared backing array via an `append` with spare capacity
- Uses a three-index slice expression (`finalArgs[:len:len]`) to cap the slice capacity, forcing `append` to allocate a new array
- Adds a regression test that confirms the args slice is not corrupted during shell completion

## Details

When shell completions are requested (e.g., `prog __complete x`), `getCompletions()` calls:

```go
_ = finalCmd.ParseFlags(append(finalArgs, "--"))
```

`finalArgs` is a sub-slice of the original args (derived from `os.Args[1:]`), and if it has spare capacity in its backing array, `append` writes `"--"` directly into the shared memory rather than allocating a new slice. This corrupts `os.Args`, which users may be inspecting in their `ValidArgsFunction`.

The fix uses `finalArgs[:len(finalArgs):len(finalArgs)]` to limit the capacity to the length, guaranteeing that `append` allocates a fresh backing array.

The bug is most visible with `TraverseChildren: true`, since `Traverse()` returns sub-slices that preserve the original backing array's capacity.

Fixes #2257

## Test plan

- [x] Added `TestCompletionDoesNotMutateArgs` that fails without the fix and passes with it
- [x] Full test suite passes (`go test ./...`)

query.intent:
Allow linker to perform deadcode elimination for program using Cobra

Fixes #2015 

Cobra, in its default configuration, will execute a template to generate help, usage and version outputs. Text/template execution calls MethodByName and MethodByName disables dead code elimination in the Go linker, therefore all programs that make use of cobra will be linked with dead code elimination disabled, even if they end up replacing the default usage, help and version formatters with a custom function and no actual text/template evaluations are ever made at runtime.

Dead code elimination in the linker helps reduce disk space and memory utilization of programs. For example, for the simple example program used by TestDeadcodeElimination 40% of the final executable size is dead code. For a more realistic example, 12% of the size of Delve's executable is deadcode.

This PR changes Cobra so that, in its default configuration, it does not automatically inhibit deadcode elimination by:

1. changing Cobra's default behavior to emit output for usage and help using simple Go functions instead of template execution
2. quarantining all calls to template execution into SetUsageTemplate, SetHelpTemplate and SetVersionTemplate so that the linker can statically determine if they are reachable

See https://github.com/aarzilli/whydeadcode to help find why dead-code-elimination may not work as well as it could in your project.

Add default completion command even if there are no other sub-commands

This supersedes #1450 and #1392

When a program has no sub-commands, its root command can accept arguments.  If we add the default "completion" command to such programs they will now have a sub-command and will no longer accept arguments.
